name: Learn: Cluster Operations (etcd, static pods, drain)
description: Learn node-level cluster administration step by step — static pods, repairing a broken control-plane component, backing up etcd, and cordon/drain/uncordon for node maintenance. Hands-on with real multi-node access via docker exec.
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture + Troubleshooting (25% + 30%). Goal: node-level ops — static pods, repair a broken control-plane component, back up etcd, and cordon/drain/uncordon nodes.

questions.title: Static pod on a worker
questions.teach:
A **static pod** is run directly by the **kubelet** from a manifest file in its static-pod directory on a node — the API server is never asked to create it. The kubelet watches that directory and (re)starts the pod whenever the file changes.

The API server then shows a read-only **mirror pod** so you can *see* it with `kubectl`. Its name is always `<pod-name>-<node-name>`, so a pod named `static-web` on `kindlab-worker` appears as `static-web-kindlab-worker`.

**How the kubelet finds the directory**
- The path comes from `staticPodPath` in the kubelet config (usually `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`) — by convention `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`, but confirm it rather than assume.
- After editing kubelet config you must `systemctl restart kubelet` for the change to take effect; dropping a manifest in the already-configured dir needs no restart.

**Working with static pods**
- Create = write the YAML file into the dir; **delete = remove the file** (`kubectl delete pod` only kills the mirror; the kubelet recreates it from the file).
- The mirror pod is read-only via the API: you **cannot** `kubectl edit`/`apply`/`scale` it — edit the file on the node.
- Static pods have no controller; `replicas`, Deployments, etc. don't apply. One file = one pod.

**Exam gotchas**
- Target the right node — the file must live on the node where you want the pod; a worker's static pod won't appear if you wrote it on the control-plane.
- The pod name you see is always suffixed with the node name; grading usually checks `<name>-<node>`.
- The control-plane's own apiserver/scheduler/controller-manager/etcd are static pods in this same dir (next step).
- `kubectl run --restart=Never` makes an API pod, not a static pod — don't confuse them.
questions.prompt:
On worker node `$W1`, create a static pod named `static-web` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) by writing a manifest into `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on that node. Wait for the kubelet to start it.

Target: the mirror pod `static-web-$W1` is `Running` in the `default` namespace.
questions.hint: `docker exec -it $W1 bash`, then write `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml` with `metadata.name: static-web`. The kubelet picks it up within ~15s; check with `kubectl get pod static-web-$W1`.
questions.solution:
docker exec -i "$W1" sh -c 'cat >/etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF'
kubectl get pod static-web-"$W1" -n default -w   # wait for Running

verification.description: static pod manifest (name: static-web) present on $W1

questions.title: Repair a broken control-plane component
questions.teach:
The control-plane components (apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd) themselves run as **static pods** on the control-plane node, from `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`. A bad command-line flag makes a component crash-loop, and the kubelet keeps restarting it.

To fix one: edit its manifest on the node, remove/correct the offending line, and the kubelet auto-restarts the static pod — no `kubectl apply` needed. Changing the file is detected within ~15–20s.

**Diagnosing which component / why**
- `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide` — spot the `CrashLoopBackOff`/not-Ready component.
- `kubectl -n kube-system describe pod <name>` and `kubectl -n kube-system logs <name>` — but if the apiserver itself is down, `kubectl` won't work at all.
- On the node (crictl talks to the container runtime, not the API): `crictl ps -a` to find the exited container, `crictl logs <id>` for the error, `crictl inspect <id>` for the command line.
- Kubelet-level failures (bad YAML, image pull) show in `journalctl -u kubelet`.

**Common breakage classes to recognize**
- Bad/unknown flag or typo in `command:`/`args:` → container exits immediately.
- Wrong file paths in `volumeMounts`/`hostPath` (certs, config) → startup errors.
- Wrong `--etcd-servers`, ports, or `image:` tag.
- Malformed YAML in the manifest → kubelet refuses to start the pod (check `journalctl`).

**Exam gotchas**
- Edit the manifest **on the node** (via `ssh`/`docker exec`), not with `kubectl edit` — mirror pods are read-only.
- **Back up the manifest first** (`cp kube-scheduler.yaml /tmp/`) before hacking on it so you can revert.
- Moving a manifest *out* of the dir stops the component; moving it back restarts it (a handy way to force a clean restart).
- Watch indentation when editing YAML — a stray edit that breaks YAML gives a silent failure visible only in kubelet logs.
questions.prompt:
Setup has injected a bogus flag into the **kube-scheduler** static pod manifest on `$CP`, so the scheduler crash-loops. Fix `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` so the scheduler becomes healthy.

Target: the `kube-scheduler-$CP` pod in `kube-system` is Ready again.
questions.hint: `docker exec -i $CP sh -c 'grep -n bogus /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml'` to find it, then delete that line with `sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' ...`. Wait ~15s for the kubelet to restart it.
questions.solution:
docker exec -i "$CP" sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-scheduler-"$CP" -w   # wait for Ready (1/1)

verification.description: kube-scheduler static pod is Ready again

questions.title: Back up etcd
questions.teach:
**etcd** is the cluster's key-value store — all object state lives there, so a backup is your disaster-recovery lifeline. You take one with `etcdctl snapshot save`, pointing at etcd's endpoint and authenticating with its CA/client certs (found under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/`).

The etcd pod already ships `etcdctl` and the certs. Its image is **distroless (no shell)**, so call `etcdctl` *directly* via `kubectl exec` — not wrapped in `sh -c`. Save into `/var/lib/etcd` (mounted on the node), then copy the file out to `/opt/snapshot.db`.

**The four things every etcdctl call needs**
- `ETCDCTL_API=3` — the v3 API; it's the default on etcd 3.5+, but set it explicitly if unsure.
- `--endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379` — etcd's client port.
- `--cacert`, `--cert`, `--key` — the CA plus a client cert/key. On a kubeadm cluster these are under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/` (`ca.crt`, `server.crt`/`healthcheck-client.*`, `server.key`). The exact paths are also in the etcd manifest's `command:`.

**Save vs restore**
- Save: `etcdctl snapshot save <file>`; verify with `etcdctl snapshot status <file> -w table` (or `etcdutl snapshot status` on newer builds).
- Restore: `etcdctl snapshot restore <file> --data-dir=<NEW dir>` — **always restore into a fresh, empty `--data-dir`**, never the live one.
- After restore you must repoint etcd at the new dir: edit the `hostPath` volume for `etcd-data` in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml` (or stop the kubelet, swap dirs, restart). The kubelet then restarts etcd from the restored data.

**Exam gotchas**
- Distroless image → **no `sh`/`bash`**; `kubectl exec etcd-... -- sh -c '...'` fails. Call `etcdctl` directly, or run it on the node with `ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl ...`.
- Save the snapshot to a path that's actually mounted into the pod (e.g. `/var/lib/etcd`) or you can't retrieve it; then copy it to the requested host path.
- Use the **client** cert, not the peer cert; wrong certs → `context deadline exceeded`/TLS errors.
- A multi-member/stacked etcd restore must be coordinated across members; single-node kubeadm is the usual exam scenario.
questions.prompt:
Take an etcd snapshot and save it to `/opt/snapshot.db` on the control-plane node `$CP`.

Target: `/opt/snapshot.db` exists on `$CP` and is a real (non-trivial, >1KB) etcd snapshot file.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-$CP -- etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db`, then `docker exec $CP cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db /opt/snapshot.db`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-"$CP" -- etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db
docker exec "$CP" cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db /opt/snapshot.db

verification.description: snapshot is a real (non-trivial) etcd backup

questions.title: Cordon and drain a node
questions.teach:
Before taking a node down for maintenance you **cordon** it (`kubectl cordon`), which sets `spec.unschedulable=true` so no *new* pods land there — existing pods keep running.

Then you **drain** it (`kubectl drain`) to evict the existing pods so they reschedule elsewhere. Drain cordons the node automatically, so the node ends up unschedulable with its workloads gone.

**The drain flags you must know**
- `--ignore-daemonsets` — DaemonSet pods aren't evicted (they're node-bound and would just be recreated); drain **errors out without this flag** if any DS pods exist, which is almost always.
- `--delete-emptydir-data` (older alias `--delete-local-data`) — required when a pod uses an `emptyDir`, since that data is lost; without it drain **refuses**.
- `--force` — needed to delete pods **not** managed by a controller (bare/standalone pods); they won't be rescheduled.
- `--grace-period` / `--timeout` / `--pod-selector` / `--disable-eviction` (use DELETE instead of the eviction API, bypassing PodDisruptionBudgets) — the usual knobs.

**How eviction behaves**
- Drain uses the **eviction API**, which respects **PodDisruptionBudgets**; a strict PDB can make drain hang/block until it's satisfiable.
- Static pods and mirror pods can't be evicted and are left alone.
- cordon/uncordon only flip `spec.unschedulable`; they never move pods — only drain evicts.

**Exam gotchas**
- `kubectl get nodes` shows `SchedulingDisabled` on a cordoned node — a quick way to confirm.
- Forgetting `--ignore-daemonsets` or `--delete-emptydir-data` is the #1 reason drain fails; read the error, add the flag, rerun.
- After maintenance you must `kubectl uncordon <node>` — drain does NOT re-enable scheduling (next step).
questions.prompt:
Node `$W2` needs maintenance. Cordon it, then drain it (ignoring DaemonSets and deleting emptyDir data).

Target: node `$W2` is cordoned — `spec.unschedulable=true` — and the drain completed.

questions.title: Uncordon the control-plane
questions.teach:
`cordon` marks a node unschedulable (no *new* pods); `uncordon` reverses it by setting `spec.unschedulable=false`. After node maintenance you uncordon to return it to service.

**What uncordon does and doesn't do**
- It only makes the node schedulable again — it does **not** pull back the pods that drain evicted; the scheduler places *new* pods there over time.
- Pods already running elsewhere stay put; nothing is rebalanced automatically.

**Control-plane specifics**
- Control-plane nodes can be cordoned/uncordoned like any other; their **static** control-plane pods keep running regardless of `unschedulable` (static pods ignore the scheduler).
- Control-plane nodes normally carry the taint `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule`, so ordinary pods won't land there even after uncordon unless they tolerate it — a separate mechanism from cordon.

**Exam gotchas**
- `cordon`/`uncordon` take a **node** name, not a pod; `uncordon` is idempotent (safe to run on an already-schedulable node).
- `kubectl get node <name>` should no longer show `SchedulingDisabled` once uncordoned.
- Distinguish the two blockers: `unschedulable` (cordon) vs a **taint** — removing one doesn't remove the other.
questions.prompt:
The control-plane node `$CP` was cordoned for maintenance. Bring it back into service.

Target: `$CP` is schedulable again — `kubectl get node $CP` no longer shows `SchedulingDisabled`.
